City Block Hunt

LogicGame StrategyCounting
Game: A treasure is hiding under one square of the grid; find it by touching squares.
How to play: Touch a square to learn how many blocks away the treasure is. Turn on the hint to see which squares are still possible, then keep guessing until you find it.
Look for the math

One number from each square seems like very little to go on. Yet two well-chosen touches are always enough to pin down the treasure, while ten touches can still leave you guessing. The trick is to read each clue as a whole line of possible squares, not as a single answer.

Count the blocks

The clue is the taxicab distance: walk only along the grid lines, never diagonally. From square (c, r) to (c', r') it is |c - c'| + |r - r'|. So a clue of 0 means you have landed on the treasure and the hunt ends. The original applet stored its treasure as a Java Point with the column and row swapped when it worked out this distance; both numbers were chosen at random, so the swap changes nothing about the game.

One clue is a diagonal

Touch the top-left corner (0, 0). The squares at distance d from it are exactly those with c + r = d — a descending diagonal band. Now touch a neighbouring corner, (n-1, 0). Its clue is (n-1-c) + r. The two clues give c = (d1 - d2 + n - 1)/2 and r = d1 - c, so the square is fixed. Two touches always suffice — the logic test checked every treasure on every board from 2 by 2 up to 8 by 8. The magazine's answer of two was right; the extra idea on the page is that the two diagonals simply cross at the treasure. One touch of a corner is the page's "which diagonal" step; this port also offers a hint that outlines the squares each clue still allows.

When clues are not enough

Two treasures can be confused only if every square you touch gives the same distance to both. On a 4 by 4 grid the pair (0, 1) and (1, 0) agrees on ten squares, so you can touch all ten and still not know which one hides the treasure. That answers the page's first question: 10, not the 4 the magazine guessed. On an n by n board the largest such set is n² - 2n + 2 — 10 at n = 4 and 50 at n = 8 — and an eleventh touch always breaks the tie on the small board. The invariant here is the equal-distance set: a clue cannot tell apart two cells that lie on the same kind of line from it.

Try the two-corner opening: touch the top-left square, then the top-right one, and see whether the remaining highlighted squares collapse to a single cell. Then switch the board to 8 by 8 and try it again.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
